get.description:
The read half of the term API, which was missing. This surface has had term POST, PATCH and DELETE since taxonomy writes shipped, and no GET of any kind — so a term could be created and updated but never listed, and the only way to see what a taxonomy contained was to pull the whole directory root. Convention Grid hit exactly that reworking 66 industry terms.

**`listingCount` respects your key.** A key without `read:drafts` gets the count of listings it can actually fetch — published, plus drafts whose `publishAt` has passed — and `listingCountIncludesDrafts` says which you were given. This matters more than it sounds: CourseAlmanac holds 14,470 listings and one published, so an unscoped count would render "Golf Courses (14,470)" above a list of one.

**Not paginated.** A taxonomy is an operator-curated set: the largest on the platform holds 141 terms and all of them together hold 614. The directory root already returns every term in one payload.

**To list the listings tagged with a term, use `GET /directories/{directory}/listings?terms={slug}`** — that already exists and takes comma-separated slugs (matching ANY of them).

patch.summary: Add and remove a listing's taxonomy terms without sending the whole set
patch.description:
Requires `write`. Body is `{ "add": [{ taxonomy, term }], "remove": [...] }`; either key may be omitted, but not both.

**Why this exists alongside `PUT`.** `PUT` is replace-all, so the documented way to add one tag is to read a listing's terms and send them back with the new one appended. That is not safe under concurrency: two overlapping read-modify-write cycles each send a complete set, and the later write discards the other's addition. Nothing errors, nothing is logged, and the listing quietly stops appearing under a category. Replace cannot express "add this one tag", so no amount of caller care fixes it.

`PUT` is still the right call for an authoritative full sync, e.g. an importer that owns the whole set.

**Idempotent.** Adding a pair the listing already has, or removing one it does not, is a no-op rather than a conflict — so a retried request is safe. A slug that does not exist in this directory is still a 400, including in `remove`: a typo'd removal that silently removed nothing would report success for work it did not do.

The same pair in both `add` and `remove` is a 400. Either order is defensible in isolation, so picking one would silently resolve a bug in the caller's diff.

The response carries the listing's **full resulting term set**, read back after the write — not an echo of the request — so no follow-up GET is needed and a delta that collided with a concurrent write cannot report a set it did not produce.

post.summary: Queue site probes for this directory’s listings
post.description:
Plain HTTP — no browser, no rendering cost.

**Two kinds, and neither implies the other.** `kind: "link"` (the default) checks whether each URL resolves, keyed per URL, and is what `dead-links` reports on. `kind: "site"` captures what the page says — title, description, headings, body text, signals — keyed per host and shared across directories.

A directory can have every URL confirmed alive and no captured content at all, so `queued` on its own does not tell you which half of the pipeline has run. The response echoes `kind`.

**Queued by distinct URL, not per listing.** Forty listings on one domain queue far fewer than forty jobs, and records are shared across directories, so a host another directory already probed costs nothing here.

get.description:
Joins this directory’s listings to the shared probe records.

**Only `unreachable` counts as dead by default.** A site refusing an automated client — routine behind Cloudflare — is not a broken link, and a report mixing the two teaches an operator to ignore it. 13 of EpicDirectories’ 137 sites answer 403 and are entirely healthy. Pass `includeBlocked=true` to see those as a separate concern.

`summary.urlsNeverChecked` is the **gap** in the report, not a pass: those URLs have no evidence either way until a sweep has run, and must not be read as healthy. Likewise `listingsWithoutUrl` can never be checked by anything.

**Every item names the `field` its URL came from**, and `source` says whether that was the listing’s own `canonicalFields` or an attribute opted in through `enrichmentPolicy.linkSweepAttributes`. A listing can carry several URLs, so one listing may produce several items — `summary.deadLinks` counts findings and `summary.affectedListings` counts distinct listings.

**`liveness: "endpoint"` fields are judged differently.** For a field marked that way in the policy — an API root, typically — any HTTP response of any status proves something is listening, so only an unreachable host or an explicit 410 is dead. A 404 or a 500 at `https://api.example.com/v1` is normal: it is a path prefix, not a resource. `summary.aliveByLivenessRule` counts what that suppressed, so the rule is never invisible.

**`enrichmentPolicy.linkDeadOn` widens what counts as dead.** By default only an unreachable host is — a URL whose certificate does not cover its own hostname, or which times out, is recorded as `error`/`blocked` and excluded, so it reads as ALIVE. `{ "tls": true }` counts a certificate fault; `{ "timeoutAfter": 2 }` counts a URL that has timed out that many consecutive checks — not one slow response. `summary.deadOn` echoes both, so the report can be read without the config beside it.

Reads the probe evidence already on record and applies this directory’s screening policy. **Fetches nothing** — run `POST .../site-probes/sweep` with `kind: "site"` first, or the answer is about hosts nobody has looked at.

Four verdicts, one per listing, most severe first: `site-dead`, `site-parked`, `site-placeholder`, `site-thin`.

**`summary.unscreened` is the gap, not a pass.** Those listings have no site evidence either way. `summary.inconclusive` counts hosts that refused us or that we could not reach — never a verdict, because a Cloudflare challenge is a fact about our crawler and not about the business.

post.summary: Tag the flagged listings, and hold the confident ones in draft
post.description:
Writes the verdicts as terms in the review taxonomy, creating the taxonomy and only the terms actually earned.

**Additive.** Terms are written directly, so a listing’s services, industries and regions are untouchable by this endpoint — unlike `PUT .../terms`, which is replace-all.

**Self-correcting.** A screening term that no longer applies is removed, so a site that comes back stops being tagged as dead. Only the four screening terms are ever removed; your own review tags are never touched.

**It never re-publishes.** `site-dead`, `site-parked` and `site-placeholder` pull a published listing back to draft. Nothing puts it back — a listing may have been edited or merged since, and silently re-publishing is a change nobody asked for. Pass `hold: false` for a tag-only pass.

Send `dryRun: true` to see the counts without writing. It previews both halves — `wouldTag`/`wouldHold` for what would be added, `wouldClear` for what would be removed. Watch `wouldClear`: clearing recovered listings is uncapped and is not drawn from the capped selection, so a converged directory can preview zero tags and still have removals pending.

post.description:
Unauthenticated. Requires the directory to have opted in via `submissionPolicy.reviews = true`; otherwise 404 — a directory never accepts anonymous writes by default.

Takes `authorName`, `rating` (1-5) and `body`, as JSON or as multipart.

Up to 3 images may be attached as multipart parts named `images`, 5 MB each. Every one is identified by its CONTENT rather than its declared type, then re-encoded to WebP and bounded to 1600px. **Re-encoding discards EXIF**, which is what keeps a reviewer from unintentionally publishing the GPS coordinates in a photo taken at their own home. Images attached to a submission that fails the spam checks are discarded rather than stored.

Nothing submitted here is visible to anyone until a moderator approves it, and approval is what moves the listing's rating average. The target listing is resolved through the same visibility gate as public reads, so a review on an unpublished listing returns 404 rather than confirming the draft exists.

Unauthenticated, and safe to call from a browser — it exposes no credential, no Stripe id and no redirect URL.

Returns one entry per product: `{ kind, enabled, priceCents?, currency?, name? }`.

**Render a button if and only if `priceCents` is present.** An entry with `enabled: true` and no price carries `misconfigured: true` instead — the operator has opted in and the terms are broken, so checkout would answer 503. That is reported rather than advertised.

post.summary: Start checkout for a premium listing boost (anonymous)
post.description:
Unauthenticated. Requires the directory to have opted in via `monetizationPolicy.boost.enabled = true`; otherwise 404 — a directory sells nothing by default.

Returns a Stripe Checkout URL to redirect the buyer to. **Send no body.** The price, currency and return URLs all come from the directory's own configuration, and a request carrying an `amountCents` (or anything else) is rejected with 400 rather than ignored.

The boost is permanent — there is no renewal — and a listing can therefore only be boosted once: a listing that is already premium returns 409 rather than taking money for nothing.

**Nothing is granted by this call, and nothing is granted by the buyer reaching the success URL.** The boost is applied when Stripe confirms payment over its webhook. A consumer must not treat the success redirect as proof of payment; it is reachable by anyone who knows the URL.

Rate limited to **10 per hour per IP**.

Returns a Stripe Checkout URL to redirect the buyer to. **Send no body.** The price, currency and return URLs all come from the directory's own configuration, and a request carrying an `amountCents` (or anything else) is rejected with 400 rather than ignored.

**The buyer's brief is collected ON THE STRIPE PAGE**, as up to three custom fields — the link destination, the anchor text, and either a topic (guest post) or which existing post to edit (niche edit). They come back inside the signed webhook, so a paid order always has a brief. The article copy itself does not fit a Stripe field and arrives by email.

Unlike the boost route there is **no duplicate guard**: these are repeatable, and someone may legitimately buy three guest posts.

**Nothing is created by this call, and nothing is created by the buyer reaching the success URL.** The order is created when Stripe confirms payment over its webhook. A consumer must not treat the success redirect as proof of payment; it is reachable by anyone who knows the URL.

Rate limited to **10 per hour per IP**.

info.title: EpicDirectories API
info.description:
API-first directory data platform.

**Auth:**
- `bearer` — Clerk JWT for the admin app (used by `/v1/...` routes).
- `apiKey` — `x-api-key` header for third-party integrations (used by `/public/v1/...` routes). Generate keys per-account via the admin UI. There are **five** per-key scopes: `write` (any mutation), `read:drafts` (listings that are not published), `submissions` (the anonymous submission queue), `reviews` (the public review and comment queues) and `payments` (the payment log, the order queue, and granting a boost by hand). A key with no scopes array at all is a legacy key and is unrestricted.
- Anonymous — `/v1/health` and `/v1/directories/templates`.

name.description: Display name for the new directory

domain.description: Public domain this directory is published on, as a bare hostname. A pasted URL is normalised — scheme, port, path and case are stripped, and a leading "www." is KEPT because it is part of the hostname. Null or an empty string clears it.

listingTypes.description: Listing types supported by this directory

submissionPolicy.description: Opt-in for anonymous public writes. Absent/empty accepts nothing. Keys: `suggestions`, `feedback`, `reviews`, `comments` (page comments). Each flag must be exactly true — see common/directory-open-policy.ts.

enrichmentPolicy.description:
Site-probe config. Absent = ON with defaults — unlike submissionPolicy, which is opt-in because it accepts untrusted writes. Probing writes nothing public. Keys: { probe: bool, autoApprove: bool, rubric?: string, linkSweepAttributes?: [{ key, liveness? }] }.

`linkSweepAttributes` adds this directory’s own url-typed ATTRIBUTE values to the link sweep, which otherwise checks only the one URL in canonicalFields. An explicit allowlist, in priority order — enrichment writes url-typed attributes of its own (`site_og_image`, `site_canonical_url`, `site_final_url`) that nobody wants checked, and one sweep run is capped, so something has to go first. `liveness: "endpoint"` marks a field that is a machine surface rather than a page: any HTTP response counts as alive, and only an unreachable host or a 410 is dead. An API root answering 404 is normal.

`sweepSchedule` makes the link sweep run on its own: `true` for daily, or `{ "everyHours": 24 }`. Absent means OFF, and that default is deliberate — unlike `probe`, which is on by default because a sweep only ever ran when a person asked for one. Removing the person does not keep that safe: every directory on the platform reads `probe !== false` today, so deriving the schedule from it would enrol all 74,387 listings in a perpetual crawl. `probe: false` still wins over any schedule. Catch-up after a capped run is automatic, so no cadence shorter than an hour is accepted or needed.

`linkDeadOn` decides what counts as dead beyond an unreachable host: `{ tls: true }` counts a certificate fault, `{ timeoutAfter: 2 }` counts a URL that has timed out that many checks in a row. Both default OFF and neither can be turned on globally — three Convention Grid listings have a `www.` certificate that does not cover the host while serving 200 at the apex, and that report deliberately leaves them out.

slug.description:
New slug. Renaming **preserves the old slug as an alias**: every read that addresses this listing by the old `(listingType, slug)` keeps resolving, and answers with the new slug — so a consumer can compare the two and emit a 301 instead of serving the same listing at two live URLs. `GET .../listing-aliases` returns the whole redirect map for a directory in one call.

Renaming back to a slug this listing previously used consumes that alias rather than creating a cycle. A slug held live, or held as an alias by a **different** listing, is a 409.

term.description: Term slug within that taxonomy (e.g. technology)

terms.description: Replace-all set of taxonomy term assignments by slug. Sending an empty array clears all terms.

add.description: Assignments to add, as { taxonomy, term } slug pairs. Adding a pair the listing already has is a no-op, not a conflict — so a retried request is safe.

externalId.description: Upstream record ID for dedup (e.g. Google place_id, scraper URL hash).

payload.description: Raw research/source payload to preserve in the evidence locker.

fetchedAt.description: When the underlying source data was fetched. Defaults to now if omitted.

type.description:
What to run. `geocode` uses the Google Geocoding API; `google_places` looks the listing up in Places and stores the response as a `SourceSnapshot`. Defaults to `geocode`.

`ai_description` is **not** offered: it is withdrawn, not pending.

direction.description:
Geocoding direction.
- `auto` (default) — **reverse** when the listing already has `lat`/`lng` but is missing `city`, `postalCode`, `admin1` or `country`; **forward** when it has an address but no coordinates; skipped when it has both.
- `forward` — address → coordinates.
- `reverse` — coordinates → city / admin1 / postalCode / country. This is the one you want if you geocoded client-side and only need the administrative fields filled in.

force.description: Re-geocode a listing that already has coordinates. Off by default so a re-run is cheap and cannot overwrite hand-corrected coordinates. Even with `force`, existing non-coordinate values are never overwritten — enrichment only ever fills blanks.

externalId.description:
A Google **place id**, for `type: "google_places"` only. When supplied we fetch that exact place via Place Details instead of guessing with a text search.

This is the difference between an exact lookup and a fuzzy one. Text search returns its best guess with no confidence score, so the result has to be confidence-gated — and the gate correctly refuses matches like "Business Organization Studio" → "Cozy Home Studios". If you already hold the id, that whole round trip is loss.

The gate is skipped for an id lookup, because you asserted which place this is and there is nothing left to guess. If the returned place's name disagrees with the listing, the response carries `nameMismatch` — the enrichment still applies, but a stale or mistyped id resolves to a real, wrong business and you should see that rather than have it written silently. Both `places/ChIJ…` and a bare `ChIJ…` are accepted.

kind.description:
What to check.

- `link` (default) — **does this URL resolve?** Keyed per URL, because a host-level answer cannot see a dead path on a live domain. This is what `dead-links` reads.
- `site` — **what does this page say?** Captures title, description, headings, body text and signals. Keyed per host and shared across directories, so two directories listing the same company pay for one probe.

They are not interchangeable and neither implies the other. A directory can have every URL confirmed alive and no captured content at all — which is exactly the state EpicWebDesigners was in when this parameter was added.

limit.description: How many probes to queue this run. Capped at 500 regardless of what you send — probing costs are pooled across every consumer, so one directory cannot drain the budget for the rest. The response reports `deferred` when the cap bit, and successive runs rotate: candidates are ordered oldest-checked first, so a directory larger than the cap is eventually covered rather than stuck on the same slice.

force.description:
Re-check URLs whose record is still current. Off by default, so a repeated sweep only covers what has gone stale and is cheap to run on a schedule.

Use it when the checker itself changed and existing verdicts were computed by the old one.

limit.description: How many listings to queue this run. Capped at 50 regardless of what you send — rendering is metered browser time on a shared account, so one directory cannot drain the day for every other consumer. The response reports `deferred` when the cap bit, and the next run picks up where this one stopped.

force.description:
Re-capture listings that already have a screenshot, replacing it. Off by default, so a repeated sweep is cheap and idempotent rather than re-rendering the whole directory.

**Use this when the existing capture is the problem** — a challenge page, or a blank that predates the blank-render check. The replacement is stored and live BEFORE the old asset is removed, so a failed re-capture leaves the current screenshot in place rather than clearing it.

width.description:
Width of the `site` variant for this run, in pixels. **Send this alone and the height follows the capture's 3:2** — 400 becomes 400x267, 600 becomes 600x400. That is almost always what you want, and computing 266.67 by hand is how a directory ends up with a variant whose aspect quietly crops every screenshot.

Capped at 1200, the renderer's own capture width: anything larger is an upscale of pixels that do not exist, which reads as a rendering bug rather than a choice.

Set `enrichmentPolicy.screenshot` on the directory to make a size stick across every sweep; this parameter is for one run.

height.description: Height of the `site` variant, in pixels. Only needed for an aspect other than the capture's 3:2 — and note that a different aspect means cover-fit CROPS, from the top. 400x252 for instance discards about 5.5% of each capture's height. Capped at 800 for the same reason as `width`.

listingSlugs.description:
Capture these listings specifically, by slug, instead of letting the sweep choose.

A named set is an **instruction**, so the retry window is bypassed — if you can see a listing has no screenshot and ask for it by name, you get an attempt. It does NOT replace an existing screenshot; pass `force` as well for that.

Use it to retry a listing whose URL you just fixed, or to re-capture a few at a new size without re-rendering the directory. Slugs that match nothing come back as `unmatchedSlugs` rather than being silently dropped. Still subject to the per-run cap.

limit.description: How many listings to queue this run. Capped at 100 regardless of what you send: each job is a request to somebody else's server, and a directory with ten thousand listings must not be able to point a burst that size at one host. The response reports `deferred` when the cap bit, and the next run picks up where this one stopped.

force.description: Re-read every listing regardless of how recently it was last read. Off by default, so a repeated sweep costs only the listings that have gone stale rather than re-fetching the whole directory.

staleAfterDays.description: Treat data older than this many days as stale and re-read it. **This is the knob for periodic refresh** — run the same sweep on a schedule and it re-reads only what has aged past the window. `0` means "everything is stale", which is `force` by another name.

sources.description:
Which sources to gather from. Defaults to `site` alone.

Each writes into fields prefixed with its own name — `site_title`, `google_rating` — so two sources describing the same thing can never overwrite each other. That convention exists because the unprefixed form already went wrong: a bare `rating` held 2,418 values from a partner import and one from Google, with nothing recording which was which.

**`google_places` is billable.** Google charges per request, where `site` costs only a fetch, so it is never included by default — a sweep over thousands of listings has to ask for it. Matches are confidence-gated: Places returns its best guess with no score, and a listing whose title is not really a place would otherwise be attached to an unrelated nearby business.

declareFields.description:
Create the attribute templates these sources write into, if the directory has not declared them already.

**Send this once, on your first call.** Research only writes into fields the directory has declared — without a template for `site_title` there is nowhere for the title to go, and the sweep succeeds while writing nothing. This declares all of them in one step instead of eleven separate calls.

Templates it creates are marked `{ derived: true, source }`, which is what allows later sweeps to refresh them. **Templates that already exist are left exactly as they are** — if you declared `site_title` yourself and filled it in by hand, this will not quietly convert it into a field a sweep may overwrite.

ingestOg.description:
Fetch each page's og:image and store it as a `site_og` media asset, rather than keeping only the URL. **On by default.**

The URL alone means every image you render is a hotlink to someone else's CDN. These are marketing sites — they redesign, change host, and rotate cache-busting paths, and when they do your listing shows a broken image with nothing to say it happened. Importing once makes the bytes yours.

Costs one fetch and one stored image per listing, so set `false` if you only want the text fields. A listing that already has a `site_og` is left alone — re-running updates the `site_og_image` field but never replaces the stored asset.

listingSlugs.description:
Research these listings specifically, by slug, instead of letting the sweep choose.

A named set is an **instruction**, so the staleness window is bypassed — asking for a listing by name gets it re-read. Unlike a screenshot this destroys nothing: each read is stored as its own snapshot, so the previous evidence survives.

Slugs that match nothing come back as `unmatchedSlugs` rather than being silently dropped. Still subject to the per-run cap.

dryRun.description: Report what would change and write nothing. The counts are computed by the same code path that does the writing, so a dry run cannot disagree with the real one.

hold.description: Pull flagged listings back to draft as well as tagging them. On by default: which verdicts unpublish is a property of the policy, not of the caller. Set false for a tag-only pass when you want to read the queue before anything leaves the directory.

limit.description: How many listings to act on, capped at 2000. The response reports `deferred` when the cap bit rather than implying full coverage.

url.description: Publicly reachable http(s) URL of the image. We fetch it server-side, store the original in R2, and queue variant generation — so the asset survives the source URL going away. The asset is created with `status: "pending"` and flips to `ready` once the original is stored; poll `GET .../media` to watch for it. `data:`, `file:` and private/link-local addresses are rejected with 400.

source.description: Where the image came from, for provenance — e.g. `official_site`, `google_places`, `operator_supplied`. Free-form; defaults to `url`.

alt.description: Alt text. Set it here — it is the one media field that affects both accessibility and image SEO, and it cannot be inferred from the file.

caption.description: Human-readable caption rendered near the image.

role.description: Disambiguates what the asset is FOR — consumers pick the page hero by this rather than by position. Closed set; anything else is rejected with 400 rather than silently stored.

sortOrder.description: Display order within the listing, ascending. Ties break on createdAt.

source.description: Source of the media (e.g., upload, google_places, yelp)

sourceRef.description: Reference to source (URL or external ID)

alt.description: Alt text for accessibility + image SEO. Pass empty string to clear.

caption.description: Caption rendered alongside the image. Pass empty string to clear.

role.description: Asset role on the listing — disambiguates which image is the page hero vs the brand logo vs a gallery image.

sortOrder.description: Display order within a listing (ascending). 0 first.

externalId.description: External ID from the source system

payload.description: Raw payload data from the source

fetchedAt.description: When the data was fetched from source (ISO 8601)

isPrimary.description: Set as primary domain for this directory

spam.description: Mark as spam rather than merely rejected, so abuse triage can separate the two.

path.description: The page being commented on, as a path: `/herbs/ginger/`. Query string and fragment are stripped, it is lowercased, repeated slashes collapse, and a trailing slash is added unless the last segment is a file (`/feed.xml`). Only `a-z 0-9 / . _ ~ -` are allowed.

authorName.description: Display name the commenter chooses. Unverified — there is no end-user auth, so this is text, not an identity, and consumers must render it as such.

body.description: The comment itself. Plain text — render it escaped.

email.description: Commenter email, for follow-up. Never published.

turnstileToken.description: Cloudflare Turnstile token from the widget.

spam.description: Mark as spam rather than merely rejected, so abuse triage can separate the two.

reply.description: The editors' public reply, shown beneath the comment once it is approved. `null` or an empty string clears it.

replyAuthor.description: Who the reply is from, as readers should see it, e.g. "The editors".

status.description: `refunded` is deliberately not accepted. A refund is Stripe's fact and arrives over the signed webhook, which sets it; a status typed here could claim money went back when it did not. An order already refunded answers 409 to any status change.

placementUrl.description: Where it was published. **Required in order to reach `delivered`** — it is the only field that lets anyone but the operator confirm the buyer got what they paid for. Send an empty string to clear it, which is refused while the order is delivered.

operatorNotes.description: Operator-only. Never rendered publicly. Empty string clears it.

purchaserEmail.description: Who the work is discussed with. Not validated as an email: this is a note to the operator, and nothing sends mail to it — there is no email infrastructure in this system.

targetUrl.description: Link destination the post should point at.

brief.description: Topic, a link to a draft, or instructions.
